newsitem.title: SWEDEN: Corruption linked to low newspaper circulation.
newsitem.headline: Corruption linked to low newspaper circulation.

text.p: Countries with the highest newspaper circulation also generally appear to be the least corrupt, according to a new report by corruption watchdog Transparency International (TI).

New Zealand, the Nordic countries and Canada topped TI's annual list of countries perceived to be the least corrupt in the world, and were also among those where the most daily newspaper copies were published -- between 30 and 61 per 100 people.

Far down on the list were Colombia, the Philippines, Indonesia and India, which ranked poorly in the TI corruption index and where only between two and six daily papers were printed a day per 100 people.

"Corruption -- petty or grand -- thrives in a climate of secrecy," Peter Eigen, chairman of Berlin-based TI, said as he presented the study late on Tuesday to an annual forum organised by the International Institute for Democracy and Electoral Assistance.
"Thus the best conditions for bribery and extortion are those in which the media fails or is unable to perform as a watchdog for the public interest."
Every year TI calculates an index reflecting businesspeople's perceptions of how widespread corruption is.
TI's 1996 index, published in April, indicated New Zealand was perceived as least corrupt with a score of 9.43 out of 10, followed by Denmark (9.33) and Sweden (9.08).
At the bottom were Kenya (2.21), Pakistan (1.00) and Nigeria (0.69), where corruption was seen to be most widespread.

The United States, where 24 newspapers are printed per 100 people, ranked 15th in the list of perceived corruption, but Japan only ranked 17th despite a high newspaper circulation of 58 per 100 people.

TI said its study showed the two countries best known for controlling corruption in the developing world in the course of the past generation, Hong Kong and Singapore, also had high newspaper circulations.

In Singapore, 34 newspaper copies were printed per 100 people. Hong Kong, which ranked 18th in terms of perceived corruption, had the highest circulation of all the 36 places surveyed, with 82 per 100 people.

"The three countries in Western Europe with the highest perceived degree of corruption -- Italy, Spain and Greece -- on the other hand are among the countries in Europe with the lowest number of newspapers published," TI said.
In Italy and Spain, 11 copies were printed per 100 people, and in Greece, 14.
"Given these links, TI regards the media -- and newspapers in particular -- as one of the strongest allies in the fight against corruption," TI said.
The group said it would release another study soon which will rank countries by how often their business representatives pay bribes, in an attempt to show the sources of corruption.
"Sweden and Germany are both high bribe-givers," Eigen said.
TI is a non-profit, non-government organisation set up in 1993 by Eigen, a former World Bank director, to fight corruption in international business.
